routes.description: Establish Christian theism as the more reasonable account by combining cosmological, fine-tuning, moral, historical, and experiential evidence.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the principal observations are substantially more expected under a personal, morally good creator revealed through Jesus than under skeptical atheism.

motionBridge.description: The cumulative evidence makes Christian theism more reasonable than skeptical atheism.

centralBridges.description: A finite universe requires a transcendent personal cause.
Life-permitting fine-tuning is better explained by intelligent design than necessity or chance.
Objective moral values and duties require and disclose a morally good divine ground.
The principal historical facts about Jesus are best explained by his resurrection.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Immediate religious experience can provide non-inferential knowledge of God.
The independent evidential strands reinforce a specifically Christian conclusion cumulatively.

routes.description: Defeat the comparative case by exposing underdetermination, weak probability assignments, natural alternatives, and the unreliability of sectarian belief methods.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the cited evidence neither securely establishes a transcendent mind nor discriminates Christian theism from natural, unknown, or rival supernatural explanations.

motionBridge.description: The presented evidence does not make Christian theism more reasonable than skeptical atheism.

centralBridges.description: Cosmology does not establish an absolute beginning, universal causal premise, or personal cause.
Fine-tuning probabilities and designer inferences are underdetermined by immature physics and alternatives.
Moral realism and human value are not shown to require a divine ontological ground.
Dependent and partisan resurrection sources do not warrant a miraculous explanation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Religious belief-forming methods generate incompatible conclusions and therefore require independent checking.
A specific Christian hypothesis bears a strong burden against numerous competing explanations.

sections.title: Cosmic beginning, causation, and personal agency
sections.rationale: The cosmological argument supplies the proposed creator, while the reply disputes each transition from beginning through causation to an unembodied mind.

proMoves.speaker: William Lane Craig
proMoves.proposition: A finite past and contemporary cosmology establish that the universe began, and its transcendent cause must be an unembodied personal mind.

sourceSpan.excerpt: the universe is not eternal in the past but had an absolute beginning ... the transcendent cause of the universe is an unembodied mind

proMoves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted opening address is introduced as Craig's speech and uses his announced first argument.

response.rationale: This is the opening constructive statement of the cosmological route and therefore has no earlier selected target or response component.

precisionFindings.rationale: The syllogism is recoverable, but local universe, global physical reality, and the scope of causation are not consistently distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The asserted necessary progression to a personal cause exceeds the supplied support for an absolute beginning and the exhaustive two-candidate claim.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The core syllogism is valid, but the moves from finite past to cause and from cause to personal mind retain material bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Borde-Guth-Vilenkin result and philosophical examples are relevant, but their scope and the exclusion of rival causes are underdefended.

responsiveness.rationale: As an opening constructive, it clearly advances its adopted burden without needing to answer an earlier selected move.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central cosmological bridge, though it does not alone establish the complete Christian motion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move does not materially depend on representing a live opposing argument.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 161–257 contain the finite-past argument, BGV discussion, causal syllogism, and proposed personal-cause inference.

conMoves.speaker: Peter Millican
conMoves.proposition: Experience supports only physical causation within an existing world, current cosmology does not establish a global beginning, and neither premise warrants an unembodied mind.

sourceSpan.excerpt: I've never experienced things coming into existence from nothing ... there is no contradiction in supposing that the global universe is infinite in the past

conMoves.attributionBasis: The span occurs in Millican's introduced opening address and explicitly reconstructs and challenges Craig's cosmological premises.

components.text: The universal causal premise applies to creation from nothing and to the universe as a whole.
An abstract object and an unembodied mind exhaust the possible transcendent causes.

response.rationale: Millican directly contests the causal generalization and global-beginning scope, but this selected span does not fully answer the later exhaustive-candidate inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinctions between local and global universe, physical causation, and creation ex nihilo are expressly identified and consistently maintained.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move argues that confidence is unavailable and repeatedly marks speculative cosmology and limits on extrapolation rather than claiming disproof.

charity.alternative: Craig's argument is a valid syllogism whose premises aim to cover creation ex nihilo and the whole universe.
charity.decisiveQualification: Logical validity does not establish the disputed causal premise, global beginning, or personal-cause conclusion.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The scope and composition objections form a stable route from limited causal evidence to underdetermination of the cosmic conclusion.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The appeal to causal experience and cosmological alternatives is pertinent, though the quantum-particle characterization and some physical claims need qualification.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the decisive causal and scope premises but leaves the selected personal-candidate exhaustion component unanswered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The reply directly attacks the central cosmological bridge rather than merely raising a peripheral concern.

representationalCharity.rationale: It explicitly grants the syllogism's validity and separates that concession from its challenges to the premises and scope.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 800–897 distinguish rearrangement from creation, physical from transcendent causation, parts from wholes, and local from global beginnings.

sections.title: Fine-tuning probabilities and designer discrimination
sections.rationale: Both speakers treat the apparent physical coincidences as significant, but dispute their probability basis, available alternatives, and fit with the Christian hypothesis.

proMoves.speaker: William Lane Craig
proMoves.proposition: The narrow life-permitting range of constants and initial conditions exhibits specified improbability best explained by intelligent design.

sourceSpan.excerpt: there are only three possible explanations ... physical necessity chance or design ... therefore it is due to design

proMoves.attributionBasis: The opening speech explicitly labels this as Craig's second argument and presents its alternatives and conclusion continuously.

response.rationale: This selected span constructively introduces the fine-tuning inference and has no preceding selected target requiring response.

precisionFindings.rationale: The design inference is recoverable, but probability, possible range, and independence from laws remain only partly specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical three-option framing and rejection of chance outrun the supplied probability measure and treatment of multiverse or deeper-law alternatives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The abductive structure is intelligible, but the exhaustive trilemma and transition from life-permitting pattern to agency need material defense.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific constants and initial conditions are invoked, but no probability measure or representative comparison among designer hypotheses is supplied.

responsiveness.rationale: The constructive clearly advances its own fine-tuning burden without an earlier selected reply target.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central design bridge but does not by itself discriminate a Christian or morally good designer.

representationalCharity.rationale: No developed opposing alternative is represented within this opening move.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 258–323 state the fine-tuning data, the necessity-chance-design trilemma, specified-pattern warrant, and designer conclusion.

conMoves.speaker: Peter Millican
conMoves.proposition: Fine-tuning is intriguing but present physics supplies no secure probability space, deeper laws or multiple universes remain live, and design does not discriminate a good Christian God.

sourceSpan.excerpt: this constitutes a phenomenon which very naturally invites explanation in terms of a cosmic scale designer ... does nothing to support the claim that God is good rather than evil

conMoves.attributionBasis: Millican's first rebuttal explicitly addresses Craig's fine-tuning argument and carefully states both a concession and objections.

components.text: The life-permitting range has a warranted probability distribution over genuine alternatives.
Physical necessity, chance, and design exhaust the relevant explanatory alternatives.
The design inference materially favors a morally good Christian designer.

response.rationale: The reply addresses the probability basis, deeper-law and multiverse alternatives, and the failure to discriminate a good designer while conceding the phenomenon's interest.

precisionFindings.rationale: The critique distinguishes conditional evidence for intelligence from evidence for omnipotence, moral goodness, or specifically Christian theism.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Millican expressly concedes conditional design relevance while emphasizing sample-size and theory uncertainty, matching the limited warrant.

charity.alternative: If fundamental constants are genuinely free, highly constrained, and physically unexplained, their life-permitting values naturally invite a designer explanation.
charity.decisiveQualification: That conditional concession does not supply a probability measure or identify the designer as omnipotent, good, or Christian.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The reply coherently separates the existence of an intriguing coincidence from its probability, explanation, and theological discrimination.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It identifies concrete theory limitations and rival explanations, although some forecasts about future physics necessarily remain speculative.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts every indispensable component, including the decisive probability premise and the specifically Christian inference.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the central fine-tuning bridge across its data, inference, and discrimination stages.

representationalCharity.rationale: It states a strong conditional version of the design argument and concedes its genuine explanatory pull before adding qualifications.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 1385–1480 give the conditional concession, probability and sample-size objections, deeper-law and multiverse alternatives, and anti-God comparison.

sections.title: Objective morality and divine grounding
sections.rationale: The moral argument is contested at both premises: whether atheism precludes objective value and whether moral experience establishes a divine ontological ground.

proMoves.speaker: William Lane Craig
proMoves.proposition: Without God objective moral values and duties would not exist, yet moral experience discloses such values and duties, so God exists.

sourceSpan.excerpt: if God did not exist objective moral values and duties would not exist ... real evil in the world actually serves to prove the existence of God

proMoves.attributionBasis: Craig identifies this as his third opening argument and presents both premises and the conclusion in one uninterrupted speech.

response.rationale: The move opens the moral route by stating its two premises and conclusion, with no earlier selected target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The deductive form is clear, but objective bindingness, value, and duty are grouped without a fully stable account of their grounding.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is presented as inescapable although the crucial claim that no nontheistic moral ground is available is supported selectively.

charity.alternative: Naturalistic accounts explain moral behavior through evolution and social conditioning while some atheists deny deeper objective bindingness.
charity.decisiveQualification: This does not represent the strongest nontheistic realist accounts that accept objective moral truths.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument is deductively valid, but the first premise requires a substantial bridge from naturalistic genealogy to absent objective normativity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Moral experience and selected testimony support the premises only partially and do not compare serious secular-realist alternatives.

responsiveness.rationale: As a constructive, it clearly advances the adopted moral burden without a prior selected target.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central moral bridge linking a good divine ground to the motion.

representationalCharity.rationale: Its naturalistic reconstruction leans on error-theoretic and evolutionary accounts while omitting stronger atheist moral realism.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 324–406 define objectivity, present evolutionary genealogy, appeal to moral apprehension, and infer God from objective evil.

conMoves.speaker: Peter Millican
conMoves.proposition: Many nontheists are moral realists, and Craig has not explained why objective values, intrinsic human worth, or their apprehension ontologically depend on God.

sourceSpan.excerpt: 56.3% ... were moral realists but only fourteen point six percent were theists ... I don't understand ... why an atheist cannot believe in objective moral values

conMoves.attributionBasis: Millican's final rebuttal explicitly returns to Craig's moral argument and sharpens his previously announced challenge.

components.text: Objective moral values and duties cannot possess an adequate nontheistic ontological ground.
Ordinary moral apprehension is trustworthy in the absence of a defeater.

response.rationale: The reply squarely challenges divine necessity and offers nontheistic value considerations, but it does not defeat Craig's separate prima-facie trust argument for moral experience.

precisionFindings.rationale: The ontological challenge is clear, though Millican openly notes that objective has several meanings and does not settle on a complete theory.

calibrationFindings.rationale: He offers counterpossibilities and requests an explanation, expressly admitting that he may not persuade everyone with his own value commitments.

charity.alternative: Craig distinguishes knowing moral truths from the ontological question of what makes them objectively valid and binding.
charity.decisiveQualification: Granting that distinction still leaves Craig to show why the ontological ground must be God rather than a nontheistic moral reality.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The reply consistently separates moral epistemology from ontology and uses that distinction to identify the missing necessity claim.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The philosopher survey establishes that nontheistic realism is a live position, but popularity alone cannot establish its adequacy.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the decisive grounding premise but leaves the independent trust-in-moral-experience component substantially intact.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The response directly attacks the central divine-grounding bridge and its claimed necessity.

representationalCharity.rationale: It accurately identifies Craig's epistemology-ontology distinction and directs the objection to the stronger ontological formulation.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 1943–2043 present survey evidence, distinguish knowledge from ontology, analyze moral perception, and offer nontheistic sources of value.

sections.title: Resurrection evidence and historical alternatives
sections.rationale: The specifically Christian bridge turns on whether the selected historical facts are securely established and whether resurrection best explains them.

proMoves.speaker: William Lane Craig
proMoves.proposition: The empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and disciples' transformed belief are widely accepted facts best explained by Jesus' resurrection, which entails God exists.

sourceSpan.excerpt: three facts recognized by the majority of historians ... there just is no plausible naturalistic explanation ... that entails that God exists

proMoves.attributionBasis: Craig's opening speech labels the historical argument, enumerates three facts, and draws the resurrection and theistic conclusions.

response.rationale: This is the first selected statement of the resurrection argument and therefore has no earlier response target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The facts and conclusion are identifiable, but majority acceptance and absence of plausible natural explanation require bounded qualifications.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The assertion that naturalistic explanations are unavailable and resurrection is amply justified exceeds the limited source comparison provided.

charity.alternative: Natural explanations include removal of the body, survival, or other nonmiraculous origins of resurrection belief.
charity.decisiveQualification: Only two brief alternatives are named, and broader psychological, legendary, and source-critical alternatives are not developed.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The abductive route is coherent, but the move from reported facts to miracle and then to the claimed divine identity needs additional bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Named scholars and alleged consensus are relevant, yet source independence, rival hypotheses, and comparative likelihoods remain compressed.

responsiveness.rationale: The opening constructive clearly advances its historical burden and has no earlier selected target.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central bridge uniquely connecting the cumulative case to Christian theism.

representationalCharity.rationale: Natural alternatives are represented mainly by two weak examples before being dismissed as universally rejected.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 410–472 identify Jesus' claims, enumerate the empty tomb, appearances, and transformed belief, reject two alternatives, and infer resurrection.

conMoves.speaker: Peter Millican
conMoves.proposition: The Gospel accounts are late, partisan, literarily dependent, discrepant, and poorly corroborated, so they provide weak grounds for inferring a supernatural resurrection.

sourceSpan.excerpt: as a basis for belief in God they seem to me to be feeble ... these are not independent reports ... none of this is reported in any other contemporary sources

conMoves.attributionBasis: Millican explicitly announces his resurrection response and develops source-critical objections in his final rebuttal.

components.text: The three claimed facts rest on sufficiently early, independent, and reliable historical evidence.
Resurrection compares more favorably than developed natural psychological or historical explanations.

response.rationale: The reply directly attacks source reliability and independence, but it does not fully develop or compare a particular natural explanation of all three claimed facts.

precisionFindings.rationale: The source-critical proposition, its scope, and the conditional concession about prior supernatural evidence are all clearly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cautious conclusion of weak evidential force generally fits, though some broad claims about authorship and dependence are asserted rather than demonstrated.

charity.alternative: Craig's case relies on three historical facts rather than treating every Gospel detail as equally necessary or reliable.
charity.decisiveQualification: Millican's focus on Gospel dependence and discrepancy does not by itself show that none of the three narrower facts is historically defensible.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from dependence, partisanship, discrepancy, and weak corroboration to reduced historical force is coherent and appropriately limited.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific source relationships and discrepancies are identified, though the span does not independently establish every historical assertion.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the decisive reliability component but does not fully answer the comparative best-explanation claim across all three facts.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the central historical bridge to specifically Christian theism.

representationalCharity.rationale: It acknowledges reasonable Gospel coherence and conditionally grants relevance if supernaturalism were independently supported.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 2048–2105 discuss dating, authorship, literary dependence, discrepancies, canon selection, and missing external corroboration.

sections.title: Burden, religious diversity, and evidential expectations
sections.rationale: The debate's comparative standard depends on whether sectarian diversity undermines religious methods and what evidence should be expected if the Christian God exists.

proMoves.speaker: William Lane Craig
proMoves.proposition: Religious diversity does not identify one uniformly unreliable method, while Craig's case uses logic, evidence, and experience; absence counts against God only if more evidence should be expected.

sourceSpan.excerpt: there is no one method which is common to all religions ... my method this evening is logic and evidence plus personal experience ... absence of evidence is not necessarily evidence of absence

proMoves.attributionBasis: Craig's introduced rebuttal expressly quotes Millican's reliability argument and answers both that argument and the evidential-absence inference.

components.text: Religious traditions substantially share belief-forming methods that generate incompatible conclusions.
The specificity of Christian theism among many alternatives warrants a stronger prior evidential burden.

response.rationale: Craig directly denies the common-method premise and offers an evidential expectation test, but he does not answer the separate many-alternatives argument for a stronger burden.

precisionFindings.rationale: The response is clear, though method shifts between religious formation generally and Craig's particular package of logic, evidence, and experience.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conditional account of evidential absence is appropriately qualified, but the dismissal of a shared religious method is asserted with limited comparison.

charity.alternative: Millican argues not that cultural origins make religion false, but that similar formation and maintenance methods yield incompatible religious beliefs.
charity.decisiveQualification: Craig recognizes that reliability formulation, although his reply narrows attention to his own debate method rather than all listed practices.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The response correctly distinguishes absence of evidence from expected-but-missing evidence and gives a coherent conditional test.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The abstract evidential test is sound, but the claim that the present evidence exhausts what should be expected from God remains underwarranted.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the decisive common-method premise but leaves the specific-hypothesis burden component unanswered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The reply directly attacks the con route's central reliability bridge rather than the whole motion at once.

representationalCharity.rationale: Craig explicitly notes that Millican is making a reliability argument rather than the genetic inference that religious belief is false.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 1088–1145 reconstruct the reliability argument, deny a single common method, identify Craig's method, and state the expected-evidence condition.

conMoves.speaker: Peter Millican
conMoves.proposition: Because culturally transmitted religious methods generate incompatible beliefs and Christian theism is one highly specific hypothesis among many, it bears a strong evidential burden.

sourceSpan.excerpt: if some method of acquiring beliefs leads to lots of different and conflicting beliefs then that method obviously cannot be relied on ... unless his case is overwhelmingly strong we should not believe

conMoves.attributionBasis: The span occurs in Millican's opening address, anticipates the genetic-fallacy objection, and states his burden conclusion explicitly.

response.rationale: This is Millican's opening constructive statement of the religious-reliability and comparative-burden route, so it has no earlier selected target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reliability and burden propositions are recoverable, although method groups several different practices whose similarity is not fully specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The argument cautiously disclaims a genetic inference, but its demand for an overwhelmingly strong case exceeds the informal allocation of priors supplied.

charity.alternative: Christian belief might be true despite weak cultural origins, and Craig may offer logic and public evidence independent of those origins.
charity.decisiveQualification: Millican expressly grants possible truth and directs the objection to method reliability and comparative burden rather than falsity by origin.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move coherently separates genetic falsification from an undercutting reliability argument and then connects specificity to evidential burden.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Geographic variation, incompatible traditions, and dependence of thought on brains are relevant, but the implied prior distribution is not rigorously established.

responsiveness.rationale: As an opening constructive for the con route, it substantially develops its own burden without an earlier selected response target.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move centrally supports the con reliability bridge and approaches the motion-level comparative standard.

representationalCharity.rationale: It anticipates the strongest genetic-fallacy objection, explicitly rejects that weaker inference, and preserves the possibility that Christianity is true.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Events 674–790 distinguish genesis from reliability, compare conflicting traditions, discuss evidence for disembodied intelligence, and state the strong-burden conclusion.

pro.rationale: No distinct debate-wide consequence remains uncaptured by the selected moves, response links, importance judgments, section weights, or ratings.

eligibility.completionCriterion: The pro route must comparatively connect the cumulative evidence to specifically Christian theism.
eligibility.distinctConsequence: No separate eligible consequence was identified beyond the argument-specific strengths and omissions already represented.
eligibility.counterfactual: Removing the already scored argument-specific findings would not leave an independent debate-wide completion consequence.

con.rationale: No distinct debate-wide consequence remains uncaptured by the selected moves, response links, importance judgments, section weights, or ratings.

eligibility.completionCriterion: The con route must show that the evidence fails to discriminate Christian theism from skeptical alternatives.
eligibility.distinctConsequence: No separate eligible consequence was identified beyond the surviving objections and gaps already represented in move-level fields.
eligibility.counterfactual: Removing the already scored objections would not reveal an additional independent debate-wide burden consequence.
